sections.title: Dutch Design, Global Horizons: Your Degree in the Netherlands
paragraphs: The Netherlands has long been a meeting-place of ideas: a small, maritime nation whose universities have shaped science, law, trade and design for four centuries. Today it combines that intellectual heritage with a modern, internationally minded education system, in which problem-based learning, small-group teaching and close ties with industry are the norm rather than the exception.

sections.note: Each is a matter of substance rather than marketing. Dutch universities are publicly funded and externally accredited; teaching is interactive and expects independent thought; and the national habit of directness and equality tends to put international students at ease quickly.

sections.title: How Dutch Higher Education Is Organised
paragraphs: Dutch higher education is binary. Research universities (WO) emphasise academic theory and research; universities of applied sciences (HBO) emphasise professional practice and typically embed internships. Both award internationally recognised degrees, and a growing number of programmes at each level are taught entirely in English.

sections.title: Two routes through Dutch higher education

columns.title: Research universities
points: Bachelor’s: 3 years • BSc / BA theory and research

columns.title: Universities of applied sciences
points: Bachelor’s: 4 years • professional practice and internships
Master’s: 1–2 years • applied and professional focus

sections.note: 60 ECTS credits represent one full academic year of study.

sections.text: Teaching is organised in short blocks, with a strong emphasis on tutorials, group projects and continuous assessment. Because progress is monitored, with the university reporting study results to the immigration authority, applicants should choose a programme they can sustain, not merely the most prestigious one available.

sections.title: Admission Requirements
sections.intro: Entry standards are set by each programme, and competitive courses may require more than the minimum. In general:
rows: Secondary-school certificate recognised as equivalent to Dutch pre-university education; good grades (broadly a B average); motivation letter; references where requested
Some programmes apply selection or a numerus fixus quota, with an earlier deadline of 15 January.
A relevant Bachelor’s degree; a strong academic record (competitive courses often look for the equivalent of about 7.5 out of 10); CV, motivation letter and references
Business and management courses may ask for GMAT or GRE scores; others may ask for a portfolio or writing sample.

items.title: English-Language Proficiency
items.desc: English-taught programmes require evidence of proficiency. Typical thresholds are an IELTS Academic score of 6.0 to 7.0 overall or a TOEFL iBT score of 80 to 100, with higher scores for competitive programmes and minimum sub-scores in writing. Dutch is not required for English-taught degrees.

sections.title: Intakes and Deadlines
sections.intro: Most programmes begin in September, with a smaller number admitting students in February. Applicants from outside the EU/EEA are generally expected to apply earlier than EU applicants, to allow time for the residence permit; deadlines of 1 April to 1 May are common, although some institutions close earlier.

sections.title: From First Enquiry to Your First Lecture
sections.intro: Applications to Dutch universities are made through Studielink, the national platform, followed by each university’s own portal for supporting documents.

items.title: Shortlist
items.desc: Define your goals and shortlist programmes that fit your academic profile and career objectives.

items.title: Studielink
items.tag: Register and apply (up to four choices)
items.desc: Register on Studielink and submit your applications. You may apply for up to four programmes, with a lower limit for numerus fixus courses.

items.title: Portal
items.desc: Complete the institution’s portal: transcripts, certificates, language scores, motivation letter, CV, and any entrance assessment.

items.title: Admission
items.desc: Receive a decision. An offer may be conditional on final results or test scores; keep certified copies of all documents.

items.title: Funds
items.desc: Confirm your place, pay any deposit or tuition fee, and assemble proof of the funds required for the permit.

items.title: Permit
items.desc: The university, as recognised sponsor, applies on your behalf for the entry visa (MVV) and residence permit (VVR).

items.title: Travel
items.tag: Collect MVV, book flight, find a room
items.desc: Collect your MVV, arrange travel, secure accommodation and take out health insurance.

items.title: Settle
items.desc: On arrival, collect your residence card, register with the municipality, obtain your citizen service number (BSN) and open a bank account.

sections.title: Visa and Residence Permit
sections.intro: Indian students require two permissions for a full degree. The MVV is the provisional entry visa, collected from the Dutch representation before travel; the VVR is the residence permit, collected in the Netherlands after arrival. Because the university files both, the applicant’s principal task is to document eligibility accurately.

items.title: Admission confirmation
items.desc: An official offer of admission from a recognised Dutch sponsor institution.

items.title: Sufficient means (IND norm)
items.desc: The IND study norm for 2026 is €1,130.77 per month (excluding tuition), demonstrated in addition to the fee.

items.title: Valid passport
items.desc: Valid for the intended period of study with adequate blank pages.

items.title: Health insurance
items.desc: Adequate cover for the full stay; students who work require Dutch basic healthcare (Basisverzekering).

items.title: Screening and civil documents
items.desc: TB screening (where applicable) and civil documents such as legalised birth certificates.

sections.note: Study progress matters: The permit is linked to your enrolment. Universities typically expect students to earn at least 50% of the credits for the academic year, and report outcomes directly to the IND. Planning a realistic workload, especially if you work part-time, protects your status.

sections.title: The Cost of Studying
rows: Higher for MBA and specialised programmes
Usually salaried as employees of the university

sections.title: Living Costs
sections.intro: Housing is the principal variable. Amsterdam, Utrecht and Leiden are the most expensive cities; Groningen, Enschede, Tilburg and Wageningen are markedly cheaper.

items.title: Housing
items.desc: Student rooms and shared flats are in short supply, so apply as soon as you are admitted; most universities offer assistance.

items.title: Transport
items.desc: A bicycle (€40–150 second-hand) is the national student vehicle; public transport is efficient but costly without a discount.

items.title: Meals
items.desc: Cooking at home keeps groceries to roughly €120–250/mo; eating out costs €8–16 per meal.

sections.title: Scholarships and Funding

items.title: NL Scholarship (formerly Holland Scholarship)
items.desc: One-time grant of €5,000 for non-EEA students at participating institutions
items.meta: How to apply: Applied for through the university; deadlines usually fall between February and May

items.title: Institutional awards
items.desc: Merit-based awards such as Amsterdam Excellence, Maastricht NL-High Potential and TU Delft scholarships; some cover substantial fees
items.meta: How to apply: Competitive; check each university’s page

items.title: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters
items.desc: EU-funded awards covering tuition and a living allowance for selected consortium programmes
items.meta: How to apply: Apply directly to the programme

items.title: Orange Tulip Scholarship
items.desc: Country-specific awards, administered by Nuffic’s overseas offices
items.meta: How to apply: Availability has varied by country; confirm current status for India

sections.note: Education loans from Indian public-sector and private banks, as well as international lenders, are widely used to meet the balance. A well-prepared sponsor profile and early documentation materially improve the loan process, and EUROPA FUSION’s counsellors assist families with both.

items.title: During Your Studies
items.desc: Non-EU students may work for up to 16 hours a week throughout the year, or full-time in June, July and August, but not both. In either case, the employer must obtain a work permit before the student begins. Internships that form part of the curriculum do not require the same permit.

items.title: After Graduation (Zoekjaar)
items.desc: Graduates may apply for the Orientation Year (zoekjaar) permit within three years of graduating. It lasts 12 months, allows free employment without a separate work permit, and facilitates transition to a highly skilled migrant permit with lower salary thresholds.

items.title: Long-term residence

sections.note: Apply for the Orientation Year within three years of graduating; years spent on a study permit generally do not count towards long-term residence.

sections.text: Employers in engineering, information technology, logistics, finance and life sciences recruit actively among international graduates, and starting salaries of roughly €2,200 to €3,200 a month are commonly cited for graduate roles. Proficiency in Dutch, while not essential, widens the field considerably.

items.q: Do I need a GMAT or GRE score?
items.a: Not for every programme. Many Master’s courses do not ask for one, but some business, economics and quantitative programmes do. Always check the programme page.

items.q: Are gap years or backlogs a barrier?
items.a: Not necessarily. A gap can be explained in a motivation letter, and backlogs are assessed by the individual programme. A strong narrative and recent achievement carry weight.

items.q: Is a Dutch degree recognised in India?
items.a: Dutch research universities and universities of applied sciences are accredited, and their degrees are widely recognised internationally. Applicants who intend to return should check any profession-specific requirements.

items.q: Can I change programme after I arrive?
items.a: Switching is possible within some institutions but may affect your residence permit and study-progress record, so seek guidance from the university first.

items.q: Can my spouse or family join me?
items.a: Family members may apply for their own permits, subject to the IND’s conditions and income requirements. Please discuss your circumstances with a counsellor before applying.

items.q: When should I begin looking for accommodation?
items.a: As early as possible, ideally as soon as you receive your offer. Housing is the most common difficulty for new international students.

items.q: Will I need to learn Dutch?
items.a: Not for English-taught degrees. Basic Dutch, however, helps with daily life, part-time work and later career prospects.

items.q: How long does the whole process take?
items.a: Allow six to nine months from first enquiry to arrival, since applications, scholarships, permit processing and housing run in sequence.
